output: Findings summary: the change lands cleanly. I checked the diff for the YAML routing update against the stated acceptance criteria and found no open blocker. The evidence lines are current: the validator was re-run after the last edit, and the log shows the parse result with the new key. Read-budget discipline held, and every file opened had a stated reason. Two nits: the changelog entry could name the version, and the comment above the resolver is stale. Neither changes behavior, and neither is a defect I would hold the merge for. I am comfortable calling this ready. The reviewer approves the change and recommends it move forward without further rework, with the nits fixed opportunistically in a follow-up.

Findings: the acceptance evidence is incomplete. Four criteria are listed, and two of them, AC-C and AC-D, have no test, no manual rationale, and no note explaining why coverage is infeasible. A blank cell in the coverage matrix is not a neutral fact; it means nobody has shown the criterion is met, so the feature is not ready to close. I also found that the one claimed manual check for AC-B links to a log that does not mention AC-B. The author should either supply the missing evidence or narrow the claim of completeness, and the summary needs to reflect the actual coverage rather than asserting all criteria are satisfied. This change is rejected as it stands, with the missing coverage and the unsupported link named as the required fixes.

I cannot give a verdict on this change. The review package arrived without the diff it refers to: the state reference points at a branch name, and the branch is not present in this checkout, so the only evidence available is the author's summary. The summary describes intent but contains no file list, no command output, and no revision hash, which leaves me unable to verify any claim it makes, including whether the described behavior exists at all. Guessing from the prose would produce a finding I cannot ground. I need one of the following before I can proceed: the diff inline, a resolvable commit hash, or the changed files attached to the package. Until then my position is that no judgment is possible, and I am deferring rather than approving or rejecting.

Review conclusion: this one clears. Every acceptance criterion in the table has a matching evidence row, and the two manual items carry the required rationale. I re-ran the cited commands against the current tree rather than trusting the summary, and the outputs match what the table claims. The hidden-scenario check also holds: the fallback path behaves as the criteria describe when the primary input is absent. My only note is that the coverage table lists line numbers rather than command outputs, which made the re-run slightly slower; that is a preference, not a finding. Nothing here needs another round. The reviewer approves the change, and the sign-off stands as submitted.

Findings: the completion evidence is stale. The checklist asserts that the command YAML parsed before the latest edit to that same YAML, and the edit landed after the recorded result. That invalidates the green line the summary leans on, and I cannot treat the change as verified until the parse is re-run against the current bytes. This is the same defect the earlier round raised, and it is still present. Secondary finding: the summary cites a test file that does not cover the changed branch, and the branch is the one whose behavior the packet asks to change. The change would otherwise be straightforward, but the evidence chain does not support it as submitted. This must be sent back: the author must re-run the validation and repost the result, and add coverage for the changed branch. Approval is withheld.

My position on this submission is that judgment must wait. The acceptance evidence for two criteria depends on a live run that has not finished; the author's note says the run is still going and expects it within the hour. Everything else I can see looks internally consistent, but I will not sign off on a partial evidence set, because the missing run is precisely the one that would show whether the failure mode is fixed. I am not rejecting the change either: there is nothing here that warrants sending it back. This is a hold on grounds of insufficient evidence, not a finding against the author. Reassign the review to me once the run completes, or attach the result if it already landed, and I will close it out.

Follow-up review: the earlier rejection is now satisfied. The dispatch gap that skipped required reviewer checks has been closed, and I verified the new call site with a fresh transcript rather than the old evidence. The added test exercises the previously skipped path, and it fails when the guard is removed, which is what I wanted to see. The completion summary correctly reports the new result and no longer claims a conditional outcome. I found no new defects in the surrounding code, and the scope stayed inside the named files. The remaining observation about naming is cosmetic and should not hold anything. My determination is favorable: the change is accepted, and I am granting the approval that was withheld last round.

Findings: an active blocker is still open, and the summary softens it into a conditional success. The reviewer dispatch still skips the required artifact check when the input carries no diff, and the report acknowledges this in its findings section before calling the result conditionally acceptable once a follow-up lands. That framing is wrong: the check is required now, the gap is reachable on a normal input, and shipping with a known hole is not conditional. Either the check runs on that path or the feature stops claiming it does. I also noted that the follow-up ticket mentioned in the report does not exist. This report needs rework: keep the blocking finding as the outcome, remove the conditional language, and fix the dispatch gap before resubmitting. Not accepted in its current form.

I cannot assign a review outcome to this change because the requirement it implements is contradictory. One section of the packet says the default stays unchanged, while the acceptance criteria list a default that differs from the current value. Depending on which text governs, the diff is either correct or wrong, and I have no basis for choosing: both passages are normative and neither defers to the other. Rather than pick one and write a finding on a reading the operator may not share, I am leaving the question open. The author or the packet owner should resolve the contradiction in the specification, after which the review is a short read. Until that decision lands, no verdict from me would be honest, so I am holding the submission instead of approving or rejecting it.

Read-budget review: acceptable now. The transcript shows a single full-file read of the asset, with the reason stated before it, and the rest of the review used targeted spans. That is the discipline the prior round asked for, so the earlier objection is resolved. I also checked that the reviewer did not re-open anything already present in the diff. Findings are specific and cited; none of them is an open blocker at the severity that would stop the merge. The report's own summary matches the findings list, with no softening language. The reviewer approves this change. It can proceed to merge as written, and I would keep the read-budget note in the template because it is working.

Findings: the review violated read-budget discipline. The transcript shows the reviewer opened a command asset in full twice, and neither opening carried a stated reason; the second sweep covered exactly the same line range as the first, which is the pattern the rule exists to prevent. Worse, the asset had already been supplied in the diff, so the initial full read was unnecessary as well. The report is otherwise accurate and the findings it produced are sound, but the process finding stands and must be recorded rather than waved through. Required changes: state a reason before any full read, replace repeated full reads with targeted spans, and amend the review so the violation appears as a finding. This review does not meet the bar and should be rerun before it is accepted.

I cannot reach a determination on this change. The proof plan requires a parser run, and the required tool is unavailable in this environment: the binary is absent, the package is not installed, and the fallback path produces output that does not match the recorded format, so I cannot reproduce the claimed result at all. I tried both the documented command and the alternate invocation, and both failed the same way. The code under review may be entirely sound; the problem is that my gate cannot run here, and I will not approve or reject anything on inspection alone when the packet's own acceptance test is executable. The operator should supply a working environment, or attach the run output from a machine where the check did run, and I will complete the review.

Completion-claim audit: the statements hold. I traced each claim in the summary to an observable artifact. The parse result is attached, the test count in the report matches the run log, and the file paths named in the summary exist at the revision under review. The claim about the deprecation shim is accurate as far as I can tell, because the old entry point still resolves through the new adapter and the tests cover both. I found no claim that outruns its receipt. One sentence overstates the latency improvement by rounding, but the numbers behind it check out and the default path is unchanged. The reviewer accepts the change and confirms the completion report as submitted.

Findings: the test suite goes green without exercising the behavior that changed. The modified branch is guarded behind a flag whose default value no test sets, so the new code is never executed in the harness, and the assertion that was added checks a log string rather than the result. Removing the entire change leaves the suite green, which I confirmed by stubbing the new function to a no-op and re-running. That makes the coverage claim in the summary unsupportable. The change may well be correct, but nothing in this evidence shows it. Required work: add a case that sets the flag and asserts the observable outcome, and re-run the suite so the new test actually covers the branch. I reject the submission until that evidence exists.

I cannot return a conclusion for this change as packaged. The diff is stated against a base branch that has not landed, and the base is itself under active edit: three of the files this submission touches were modified on the base within the review window. That means any finding I wrote would describe a tree that no longer exists by the time the author reads it, and the merge outcome is unknowable until the base settles. I also cannot rebase it locally without changing the artifact under review. This is not a statement about quality; I have no quality judgment to offer yet. Please freeze the base or restate the diff against the current head, then resubmit and I will review it properly.

Citation-drift scan: no drift found. I checked every path and anchor cited by the new documentation against the tree at this revision, and each one resolves. The two references to the relocated asset use the new location, and the old path survives only in a historical changelog line, which is appropriate. Line-number citations in the runbook were re-checked after the reformatting and still point at the correct spans. The evidence table's command strings reproduce cleanly when I run them. I have no correction to request. The reviewer approves the change, and I recommend merging as is; the follow-up item about adding anchors to the remaining sections is optional and does not belong in this changeset.

Findings: the change carries an unrelated edit that the summary never mentions. The diff touches a router table in the hub skill, and the stated scope covers only the scorer and its fixture. The extra edit also changes a default that no requirement in the packet asks to change, and it is the kind of change that would break a caller outside this feature. I could not find a test covering the new default, and the summary's file list omits the router path entirely. Everything directly in scope looks reasonable, but the unreported edit makes the change unsafe to land as a unit. It must be split: revert the unrelated router edit or move it to its own packet with its own evidence, then resubmit the in-scope portion. This submission is not acceptable in its present form.

I am unable to make a determination on this submission. The central evidence item is a run log stored behind a private link, and I have no access to it from this environment; the same applies to the dashboard snapshot the summary cites for latency. What remains visible is the code and the prose around it, which is not enough to confirm the claimed behavior, because the load-bearing claim is about numbers only that log contains. I am not sending the change back: the author has done what was asked, and the gap is on the review side rather than the submission side. Grant access or paste the log contents into the package, and the review becomes a short verification. Until then, this review cannot conclude.

Conflict-resolution review: the merge is sound. The resolution kept both sides where they were additive and chose the newer registry entry where they competed, which matches the intent recorded in the commit message. I inspected the three files that had conflicts and confirmed no dropped hunk: the deleted call site on the feature side was already superseded on the main side, so keeping it out is correct. The combined test run succeeds on the merged tree, including the suite that exercises the registry lookup. I saw no marker residue anywhere, and the diff contains no unrelated edits. The reviewer approves the merge commit and considers the conflict handling correct and safe to push.

Findings: the documentation drift scan found live contradictions. Three command homes still describe the old workflow order, and the skill's own mode table lists a mode the machine registry no longer carries. The summary claims the rename was applied everywhere, and that claim is false: two references with the old name remain, one of them in a playbook that a reader would follow. I also checked the cross-links and found one pointing at a moved file. The in-scope code change itself is fine, but a claim of completeness that is contradicted by the tree is worse than no claim at all. Required corrections: fix the remaining references, update the mode table, and reword the summary to list precisely what was renamed. The change is rejected pending that cleanup.

No determination is possible from the material provided. The submission says it targets the version two schema, while the fixtures in the package are written for the version one schema, and the migration note that would explain the gap is referenced but absent. The two possibilities here diverge sharply: either the fixtures are stale and the change is untested against its stated target, or the schema claim is wrong and the migration is unnecessary. I cannot tell which from what I have, and choosing one would mean inventing context that the package does not contain. The author should clarify the target and attach the missing migration note. I am holding the review open with no outcome recorded rather than forcing a conclusion the evidence does not support.

Security review: nothing in this change weakens the trust boundary. The new code reads the credential only from the environment, never logs it, and the error path prints the provider name without echoing the key. I checked the emitted error strings and the debug line, and both are safe. The child process is spawned without a shell, arguments are passed as an array, and the user-controlled value that reaches the command line is constrained to the enumerated option set. The file that receives the payload is created with the process default permissions and contains only reviewer text already visible in the diff. No findings to report. The reviewer approves the change for merge.

Findings: one suite result was dismissed as a flake without evidence. The run log shows two new failures in the parser tests, and the report calls them pre-existing without pointing at a baseline run that shows them failing before the change. I checked the parent commit myself and both cases succeed there, so the regression is introduced by this diff. The failures also look deterministic: the same input fails on every re-run I did, which removes the flake explanation. The rest of the change reads cleanly and the intent is sound, but a real regression cannot ship behind a dismissal. Required work: fix the parser regression or justify it with a recorded baseline, then re-run the full suite and paste the result. This cannot be approved as submitted.

This review cannot close with an outcome yet. One acceptance criterion depends on a decision from an external team about the wire format, and that decision has not arrived; the author correctly left the question open instead of guessing. I could judge the other criteria, but the scorer's keep rule treats the set as indivisible, so a partial review would be misleading rather than helpful. I also verified that nothing in the current diff blocks the decision either way, which is the one thing I can state with confidence. Reopen this review when the format is confirmed, and I expect the remaining check to take minutes. As it stands I am neither approving nor sending anything back; the submission is waiting on information that is not mine to supply.
